source.title: Causal Attention with Lookahead Keys
source.authors: Zhuo-Qing Song; Peng Sun; Huizhuo Yuan; Quanquan Gu

page_placements.theme: Within-run and narrow-range loss observations have limited scaling implications

record.tranche_reason: The study measures validation loss and downstream average accuracy across several model sizes, but does not fit or test the original scaling-law equations.
record.gate_note: The paper reports validation-loss comparisons across four parameter counts at a fixed 50B-token training budget, plus loss curves over training tokens. These bear on parameter-scale loss trends, but the paper does not fit power laws or test compute-optimal allocations. Downstream benchmark averages are reported across model scales. Cited scaling-law results are not recorded as findings.
record.test_reason: This is an architecture paper proposing CASTLE attention. It cites Kaplan et al. only as background. Its experiments compare its own attention variants against a standard-attention baseline at four sizes (160M–1.3B, under one order of magnitude), all with a fixed 50B-token budget. It fits no power law, extrapolates nothing, tests no compute allocation and relates no downstream score to scale or loss. The loss and accuracy trends with size are incidental and cannot bear on any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that CASTLE and CASTLE-SWL consistently beat standard causal attention in validation loss/perplexity and in average downstream accuracy across the four scales. They add that gains are marginal at the small scale, which they attribute to limited capacity. They draw no scaling-law conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: The paper compares a new lookahead-key attention mechanism with standard causal attention; it does not reproduce the original scaling-law fitting procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported results vary by model scale and attention architecture; the paper also reports downstream outcomes under 0-shot and 5-shot evaluation.

fits_no_version.finding: At a fixed 50B tokens, validation loss falls monotonically with size for all three attention types (baseline 2.798→2.639→2.507→2.426, 160M→1.31B). Eight-benchmark average accuracy also rises monotonically with size in 0-shot and 5-shot. No functional form is fitted.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss and downstream averages improve monotonically with parameter count at a fixed token budget (incidental, unfitted).

record.problems: The validation-loss size sweep spans only 160M–1.310B parameters and does not fit a power law. It uses a fixed 50B-token training budget and reports no uncertainty estimates. Downstream average accuracy is reported, but the paper does not fit or assess a predictive relationship.
record.rows_left_out: Tables 2 and 3 report individual scores for eight benchmarks for each model and shot setting; these task-level values are omitted in favor of the paper's reported averages because the individual outcomes exceed the 60-row limit. The paper's loss curves over training tokens (Figures 6–9) are not separately rowed because no exact intermediate curve values are stated in the text.

untested.parts: No power-law fit; sizes span 160M–1.3B (<1 order of magnitude) at fixed 50B tokens; no token or compute sweep.
No depth/width variation at fixed parameter count; head-count changes serve only to match parameters.
No fitted relation of downstream accuracy to scale or loss; only four averages per architecture.

record.verdict_notes: Reader's 'tests'/T2 and V1/V6 labels are rejected: the paper is an attention-mechanism proposal, and size variation is incidental. In the 25B-token ablation, Table 13 lists Baseline-L with values identical to Baseline-M (train 2.740, eval 2.742). This looks like a copy error in the paper.

versions.untested_parts: Tests parameter-count variation at a fixed 50B-token budget over 160M–1.310B parameters; does not fit a power law, span several orders of magnitude, test bottleneck conditions, or sweep tokens or compute.
No small-run fit is used to predict substantially larger runs.
No fixed-compute-budget allocation between parameters and tokens is tested.
The study compares attention mechanisms, not depth, width, or architecture variations at fixed parameter count as a test of their effect on loss.
Only text pretraining is studied; no other modality, repeated-data regime, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling law is tested.
Reports downstream benchmark averages at four model sizes, but does not fit a predictive relationship between downstream performance and scale or pretraining loss.
No published scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal splits are refit or compared, and no curve-bending analysis is performed.

relation.reason: Kaplan et al. is cited as background in the introduction. The experiments establish no scaling-law form, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, or fitted downstream relationship.

tranche.reason: The study compares its attention mechanisms with standard attention at four model sizes and fixed training tokens. It neither fits nor uses scaling laws; its architecture comparisons report its own method's performance.

source_check.notes: All four validation losses match Table 1. The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased; these size points establish declining loss but do not establish a power law.
